:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=
  \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & -8\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system represented by the matrix.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & -8\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -8 & -8\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{8}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=0 \\ y &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=1$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+2(1)=0 
	\quad\Rightarrow\quad
	x=-2.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-2$ and $y=1.$ Or, in vector form, $\left<  -2,1 \right>.$

\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 3 & 7 \\ 3 & -2 & 4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{7}{2} \\ 3 & -2 & 4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{7}{2} \\ 0 & -\frac{13}{2} & -\frac{13}{2}\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{2}{13}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{7}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 1 & 8 \\ -1 & -2 & 3\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system represented by the matrix.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 1 & 8 \\ -1 & -2 & 3\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+1\cdot {R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & -1 & 11\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-1\cdot {R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -11\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=8 \\ y &=-11,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-11$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(-11)=8\,⇒\,x=8+11=19.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=19$ and $y=-11.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & 10 & 0\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system represented by the matrix.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & 10 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 7 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 7 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+7y &=-2 \\ y &=-1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-1$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+7(-1)=-2\,⇒\,x=-2+7=5.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=5$ and $y=-1.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}3 & -6 & 10 \\ 2 & -3 & 5\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system represented by the matrix.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}3 & -6 & 10 \\ 2 & -3 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & \frac{10}{3} \\ 2 & -3 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & \frac{10}{3} \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{5}{3}\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=\frac{10}{3} \\ y &=-\frac{5}{3},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-\frac{5}{3}$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x-2\left(-\frac{5}{3}\right)=\frac{10}{3}\,⇒\,x=\frac{10}{3}-\frac{10}{3}=0.
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=0$ and $y=-\frac{5}{3}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & -6 & -9 \\ 1 & -2 & -4\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system represented by the matrix.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & -6 & -9 \\ 1 & -2 & -4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & -\frac{9}{2} \\ 1 & -2 & -4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & -\frac{9}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-3y &=-\frac{9}{2} \\ y &=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=\frac{1}{2}$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x-3\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{9}{2}\,⇒\,x=-\frac{9}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=-3.
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=-3$ and $y=\frac{1}{2}.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-x+5y &=5 \\ x-6y &=5.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=
	\left[
	\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 5 & 5 \\ 1 & -6 & 5\end{array}
	\right].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 5 & 5 \\ 1 & -6 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -5 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -5 & -5 \\ 0 & -1 & 10\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -5 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & -10\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-5y &=-5 \\ y &=-10,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-10$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x-5(-10)=-5 
	\quad\Rightarrow\quad
	x=-55.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-55$ and $y=-10.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -55,-10 \rangle.$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider the following system of linear equations and its respective **augmented matrix**:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+6y &=-2 \\ 3x-y &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
M =
	\left[
	\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{array}
	\right]
$$

If we can convert the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form, then we can solve the system using back substitution.

The procedure for reducing $M$ to row echelon form using elementary row operations is called **Gaussian elimination**. To perform Gaussian elimination on a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we use the following procedure.

**Step 1:** Consider the entry $a_{11}=2$ of the coefficient matrix. This entry is called a **pivot element**. We want to make this entry equal to $1$. So, the first elementary row operation will be 

$$
R_1 := \dfrac{1}{2}R_1
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Consider the entry $a_{21}=3$ below the first pivot element. We want to make this entry equal to $0$. So, the second elementary row operation will be 

$$
R_2 :=R_2+(-3)R_1
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}{\color{red}1} & 3 & -1 \\ {\color{blue}3} & -1 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+({\color{blue}-3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}{\color{red}1} & 3 & -1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & -10 & 5\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, consider the entry $a_{22}=-10$. This entry is the second pivot element, and we would like to make it equal to $1$. So, the third elementary row operation will be 

$$
R_2 :=\dfrac{1}{-10}R_2
$$

and we get $M$ in row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & {\color{red}-10} & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{{\color{red}-10}}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & {\color{red}1} & -\frac{1}{2}\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+3y &=-1 \\ y &=-\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+3 \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} \right) = -1 
	\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
	x=\dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$ Or, in vector form, $\left< \dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2} \right>.$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique. In the previous example, after the first row operation we arrived at 

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}{\color{red}1} & 3 & -1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}-10} & 5\end{array}\right].
$$

This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}{\color{red}1} & 3 & -1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -\frac{1}{2}\end{array}\right]
$$

Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=3 \\ y+z &=2 \\ z &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The third equation states that $z=2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y+(2)=2 
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	y = 2-2 = 0.
$$

Now, we substitute both $z=2$ and $y=0$ into the first equation to get

$$
x+(0)+(2)=3
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x = 3-2 = 1.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x = 1,$ $y=0,$ and $z = 2.$ Or, in vector form, the solution is $\langle 1,0,2 \rangle.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the system of equations that is represented by the augmented matrix

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{array} 
	\right].
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x_1,$ $x_2,$ and $x_3.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-2 \\ {x}_{3} &=5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that $x_3=5.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(5)=-2
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_2=-2-5=-7.
$$

Now, we substitute both $x_3 = 5$ and $x_2 = -7$ into the first equation to get

$$
x_1+(-7)-(5) = 1
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_1 = 1 + 7 + 5 = 13.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x_1 = 13,$ $x_2=-7,$ and $x_3 = 5.$ Or, in vector form, the solution is $\langle 13,-7,5 \rangle.$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a System of Equations Using Back Substitution Given an Augmented Matrix

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the system of equations that is represented by the augmented matrix

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 3\end{array} 
	\right].
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x_1,$ $x_2,$ and $x_3.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-2 \\ 3{x}_{3} &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that

$$
3x_3=3 
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
	x_3=1.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(1)=-2
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_2=-2-1=-3.
$$

Now, we substitute both $x_3 = 1$ and $x_2 = -3$ into the first equation to get

$$
2x_1+(-3)-(1) = 0
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} (3 + 1) = 2.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x_1 = 2,$ $x_2=-3,$ and $x_3 = 1.$ Or, in vector form, the solution is $\langle 2,-3,1 \rangle.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 1 & 5 \\ {\color{blue}1} & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{{\color{blue}1}} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}-1} \\ -1 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & {\color{red}0} & -3 & 7 \\ {\color{blue}1} & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{{\color{blue}1}} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}-1} \\ -4 & {\color{red}0} & -5 & 4 \\ 2 & {\color{red}0} & 5 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $B$ above. By applying three matrix elementary row operations 

- $R_1 := \ldots$

- $R_3:=R_3-3R_2$

- $R_4:= \ldots$

each of the form $R_i:=R_i+kR_2,$ the matrix $A$ can be transformed into the matrix $B.$ What are the missing elementary row operations?
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To transform $A$ into $B,$ we need to make entries above and below $a_{22}={\color{blue}\bbox[lightgray,2pt]{1}}$ equal to ${\color{red}0}.$

To do this, we can apply the following elementary row operations:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{1}: &={R}_{1}-2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 & -3 & 7 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{3}: &={R}_{3}-3{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 & -3 & 7 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & 0 & -5 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{4}: &={R}_{4}+2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 & -3 & 7 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & 0 & -5 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 5 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing elementary row operations are

$\qquad$ $R_1 := R_1 - 2R_2\quad$ and $\quad R_4:=R_4+2R_2.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & {\color{blue}-3} & -1 & -6 \\ 7 & {\color{blue}-2} & -2 & -4 \\ -5 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{{\color{blue}1}} & 4 & 2 \\ -8 & {\color{blue}-3} & -6 & -4\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}-8 & {\color{blue}-3} & 11 & 0 \\ -3 & {\color{blue}-2} & 6 & 0 \\ {\color{red}0} & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{{\color{blue}1}} & {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} \\ -23 & {\color{blue}-3} & 6 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $B$ above. By applying three matrix elementary column operations 

- $C_1:=\ldots$

- $C_3:= C_3 - 4C_2$

- $C_4:= \ldots$

each of the form $C_i:=C_i+kC_2,$ the matrix $A$ can be transformed into the matrix $B.$ What are the missing elementary column operations?
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To transform $A$ into $B,$ we need to make entries to the left and to the right of $a_{32}={\color{blue}\bbox[lightgray,2pt]{1}}$ equal to ${\color{red}0}.$

To do this, we can apply the following elementary column operations:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -3 & -1 & -6 \\ 7 & -2 & -2 & -4 \\ -5 & 1 & 4 & 2 \\ -8 & -3 & -6 & -4\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}: &={C}_{1}+5{C}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-8 & -3 & -1 & -6 \\ -3 & -2 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & 2 \\ -23 & -3 & -6 & -4\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{3}: &={C}_{3}-4{C}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-8 & -3 & 11 & -6 \\ -3 & -2 & 6 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \\ -23 & -3 & 6 & -4\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{4}: &={C}_{4}-2{C}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-8 & -3 & 11 & 0 \\ -3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -23 & -3 & 6 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding elementary column operations are

$\qquad$ $C_1:=C_1+5C_2\quad$ and $\quad C_4:=C_4-2C_2.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray,2pt]{{\color{blue}1}} & {\color{blue}4} & {\color{blue}-7} \\ 2 & 2 & -8 \\ -3 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray,2pt]{{\color{blue}1}} & {\color{blue}4} & {\color{blue}-7} \\ {\color{red}0} & -6 & 6 \\ {\color{red}0} & 10 & -20\end{bmatrix}
$$

By applying elementary row operations of the form $R_i:=R_i+kR_1,$ the matrix $A$ can be transformed into the matrix $B.$ What are the elementary row operations?
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To transform $A$ into $B,$ we need to make the entries below $a_{11}={\color{blue}\bbox[lightgray,2pt]{1}}$ equal to ${\color{red}0}.$

To do this, we can apply the following elementary row operations:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -7 \\ 2 & 2 & -8 \\ -3 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{2}: &={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -7 \\ 0 & -6 & 6 \\ -3 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{3}: &={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -7 \\ 0 & -6 & 6 \\ 0 & 10 & -20\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the elementary row operations are

$\qquad$ $R_2:=R_2-2R_1\quad$ and $\quad R_3:=R_3+3R_1.$

$$

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{{\color{blue}1}} \\ -16 & -17 & {\color{blue}-4} \\ -3 & -3 & {\color{blue}-2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

By applying elementary column operations of the form $C_i:=C_i+kC_3,$ the matrix $A$ can be transformed into the matrix $B.$ What are the elementary column operations?
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To transform $A$ into $B,$ we need to make entries to the left of $a_{13}={\color{blue}\bbox[lightgray,2pt]{1}}$ equal to ${\color{red}0}.$

To do this, we can apply the following elementary column operations:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -5 & 1 \\ 8 & 3 & -4 \\ 9 & 7 & -2\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}: &={C}_{1}+6{C}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & -5 & 1 \\ -16 & 3 & -4 \\ -3 & 7 & -2\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{C}_{2}: &={C}_{2}+5{C}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 1 \\ -16 & -17 & -4 \\ -3 & -3 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the elementary column operations are

$\qquad$ $C_1:=C_1+6C_3\quad$ and $\quad C_2:=C_2+5C_3.$
